item.title: Following the herd: The push to make beef deforestation-free
item.description: It is not often that an exposé by an NGO triggers legislation to be enacted in just five years, but Colombia has achieved exactly this with its cattle traceability law.
item.dc:creator: Catherine Early
item.content:encoded: It is not often that an exposé by an NGO triggers legislation to be enacted in just five years, but Colombia has achieved exactly this with its cattle traceability law. Cattle ranching is estimated to account for 80% of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest, and an investigation in 2025 by the US-based Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) linked cattle ranching to deforestation in three of Colombia’s national parks in the biome. An earlier investigation in 2025 revealed that Colombian supermarkets purchased beef from ranchers illegally raising livestock inside national parks. Enacted in June, Colombia’s new law will require both the public and private sectors to ensure that their supply chains do not contribute to deforestation through a suite of measures, including deforestation-free certificates and ranchers installing devices such as ear tags and GPS chips on their animals. Though the legislation had a bumpy road to adoption – several previous attempts to get it signed into law failed – campaigners have been celebrating. Chris Moye, Latin American expert at EIA US, says: “It is basically the first national traceability system that, in theory, tackles the major driver of deforestation in Colombia.” Joao Gonçalves, global senior director for protein transition at campaigner group Mighty Earth said: “Ear tagging of individual animals is cheap and effective, enabling traceability from birth to market. Colombia is leading the way, and within two years its new law could make unprecedented progress in the fight against illegal deforestation.” Cattle is being taken to safety as smoke rises from forest fires burning vast swaths of the Chaco region, near Cadete Pando, Paraguay October 1, 2020. Picture taken October 1, 2020. REUTERS/Jorge Adorno Though the government has since changed hands, with Donald Trump-endorsed far right lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella taking power in August, so far there has been no sign that new environment minister Fabio Arjona Hincapié is planning to unravel the law, Moye said. The Colombian government and private sector have six months from passing the law to finalise details of how traceability systems will work. Within 18 months, it must integrate databases across the different institutions involved in implementing the law, and within two years must implement due diligence policies and practices across slaughterhouses, cattle auctions, traders and live cattle exporters. Moye acknowledges that the deadlines are demanding. “It depends on the competence of the government, and the political will. That will be the key, and I guess we'll find out.” The president’s environmental policy platform makes no mention of cattle traceability and emphasises reducing regulatory burdens, which raise questions on how aggressively the government will implement the law, he notes. Nevertheless, the platform does commit to stopping agricultural expansion into forests and strengthening environmental institutions, he adds. And cost reductions in technologies that enable the traceability of cattle and to share information between institutions make the target dates more realistic, he says. Colombia’s two-year deadline to tackle beef-led deforestation in the Amazon contrasts with the slower timetable in Brazil, home to 88% of the Amazonian herd. MANDATORY TAGGING The country has a national plan to introduce mandatory tagging of cattle and trace all movements of cattle, but not until 2032. The Amazon state of Para, host of last year’s COP30 climate conference, announced in 2023 that it would implement the scheme six years early, and would come into force in January this year. Read more However, its governor Helder Barbalho later postponed implementation of the programme until December 31, 2030, following complaints by the state’s ranchers, says Fabio Medeiros, strategic cattle partnerships director at The Nature Conservancy (TNC). Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella speaks during a press conference at San Carlos Palace in Bogota, Colombia, August 25, 2026. REUTERS/Luisa Gonzalez “Of course, it’s a setback – everybody expected Para to move forward, really before the other states. But it brings Para in line with other states, and gives producers more time to adapt,” he says. Traceability pilots are under way in Mato Grosso, Tocantins, Rio Grande do Sul and São Paulo. Other work includes engagement with smallholders to enhance productivity, and building a national platform to connect the state programmes, he says. “This is part of the movement that will cut deforestation. We expect that the implementation of traceability, and producer awareness about deforestation and the importance of compliance, will help it to move forward,” he says. There has also been a delay to a scheme requiring Brazilian banks to help combat illegal deforestation. In 2023, the Brazilian Federation of Banks (Febraban) asked members to join a self-regulatory scheme where they would ask meat processors in the legal Amazon and Maranhao regions to prove their cattle purchases did not come from areas of illegal deforestation as a condition of receiving credit. The scheme was to be implemented by December 2025, but was delayed until the beginning of 2027, Medeiros said. It was argued that it was almost impossible for producers blocked from supply chains after farming on deforested land to be relisted in supply chains, explains Medeiros. Such producers should be required to solve the problem they caused by restoring deforested areas rather than permanently punished, Medeiros says. “If producers can come back to the formal economy with obligations, this is what moves the game. Because everything that is in the past, we need to solve,” he says. Despite the delay, the scheme has already increased awareness of the issue among producers and banks, he says. Cattle stand at plant of JBS S.A, the world's largest beef producer, in Santana do Araguaia, Para state, Brazil September 11, 2025. REUTERS/Amanda Perobelli Some meat processing companies have been getting behind traceability efforts. In February, Brazil-based MBRF (formerly Marfrig) announced that it had achieved 100% traceability of its cattle supply chain, including both direct and indirect suppliers, across all Brazilian biomes where livestock is sourced. The company has monitored its direct suppliers using satellite-based tracking and geo-monitoring technologies since 2010, then announced its expansion to full monitoring of indirect suppliers in 2021. It identified socio-environmental risk levels using mapping that integrates multiple databases and classifies municipalities according to risk. “This pioneering approach made it possible to establish priority areas and a structured engagement schedule with direct suppliers to obtain information about indirect suppliers across all biomes where cattle are sourced for our production units,” according to Paulo Pianez, director of sustainability and institutional relations at MBRF. Suppliers associated with any non-compliance are automatically blocked from new cattle purchases in the company’s system until “clarifications and corrective action have taken place”, Pianez said. Though the company declined to provide absolute numbers of suppliers blocked, it said that they represented between 15% and 20% of its suppliers. Nearly 4,500 farms have been reinstated after becoming compliant, MBRF said. JBS has supported the rollout of traceability in Brazil, supplying two million electronic cattle ear tags to small ranchers in Para, in partnership with TNC. However, in June the world’s biggest meat processor revealed that it was abandoning its climate change target covering greenhouse gas emissions released into the atmosphere by suppliers, which represent the vast bulk of the company’s environmental footprint. Jason Weller, JBS global chief sustainability officer, justified the move on the grounds of difficulties in controlling indirect, or Scope 3 emissions, 92% of which are generated by the livestock it buys, according to its 2025 sustainability report. But Mighty Earth’s Gonçalves called the move “defeatist”. “JBSs’ Scope 3 emissions and deforestation cannot be addressed without knowing where cattle have been throughout their lives; traceability is therefore not peripheral to JBS’s climate commitment, it’s fundamental to delivering it.” The meat giant has shown it is capable of change, having already delivered a batch of fully traceable, deforestation-free beef to one retailer in the state of Para, he said. But Mighty Earth continued to find recent illegal deforestation in JBS’s Brazilian beef supply chains. A man picks up a piece of meat in Carrefour supermarket in Sao Paulo, Brazil November 27, 2024. REUTERS/Amanda Perobelli “The three-year delay to the rollout of the state-led traceability scheme in Para is unacceptable. Companies like JBS don’t need to wait for ambitious policy action. They have the clout and resources to require full traceability now. And retailers must insist on nothing less,” he said. Supermarkets also show mixed responses on the issue. French chain Carrefour has committed to 100% deforestation-free beef sold across all brands, including throughout the indirect farm supply chain. It has traceability and compliance in place for fattening farms across all Brazilian biomes, according to a spokesperson. Though it still needs to expand traceability to the other upstream links in the supply chain, it had already achieved this objective for own-label branded beef by the end of 2025, according to Agathe Grossmith, Carrefour’s CSR director. However, Grupo Mateus – the third-largest supermarket chain in Brazil – has been slammed by Mighty Earth for sourcing from some of the companies and slaughterhouses most connected to destruction of the Brazilian Amazon. It ranked lowest in an analysis of leading retailers and meat packers in Brazil. A spokesperson for Grupo Mateus said in a statement to The Ethical Corporation: “Throughout its 40-year history, Grupo Mateus has continuously strengthened its practices in the areas of compliance, integrity, governance and sustainability. The company reaffirms its commitment to complying with applicable laws and does not condone illegal practices within its supply chain.” Despite the setbacks in Brazil, Medeiros of TNC is upbeat about the direction of travel. “I think this is a very, very positive movement,” he says. “Some years ago, people used to say, ‘oh, it’s just Uruguay and Australia’. Now it’s not just them – it’s also Colombia, Paraguay, Argentina and Mexico – this is a mainstream approach,” he says. This article is from the latest issue of Ethical Corporation magazine, on deforestation risk. You can download the digital pdf of the magazine by clicking here

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: L'Europe termine sans direction, prudence sur l'Iran
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Europe termine sans direction, prudence sur l'Iran 28 septembre (Reuters) - Les Bourses européennes ont terminé sur de faibles variations lundi, effaçant leurs gains observés plus tôt, la prudence s'imposant face à la pression sur le marché obligataire et les cours pétroliers après le refus par Donald Trump du plan de paix iranien. BCE: Une réponse mesurée reste appropriée pour juguler l'inflation, dit Lagarde Une réponse mesurée reste appropriée pour contenir la hausse des prix, a déclaré lundi la présidente de la Banque centrale européenne, Christine Lagarde, l'inflation enregistrée cette année n'ayant pas encore entraîné d'effets de second tour dans la zone euro. TotalEnergies augmente ses rachats d'actions alors que les prix du carburant portent les bénéfices 28 septembre (Reuters) - TotalEnergies a annoncé lundi prévoir de racheter 2,5 milliards de dollars (2,20 milliards d'euros) de ses actions au quatrième trimestre 2026, contre 1,5 milliard au cours des trimestres récents, le groupe présentant sa stratégie et ses perspectives 2026 à l'occasion d'une journée des investisseurs à New York. Bill Gates appelle à son tour à mieux encadrer l'IA L'intelligence artificielle (IA) doit être encadrée bien au-delà d'un seul dispositif d'autorégulation, a déclaré Bill Gates, cofondateur de Microsoft, appelant le Congrès américain à adopter une législation en la matière. Le dirigeant d'Armani indique que la vente envisagée d'une part du groupe pourrait concerner plusieurs investisseurs Le groupe de luxe italien Armani est disposé à envisager plusieurs investisseurs pour la vente d'une participation de 15% prévue dans le testament du fondateur Giorgio Armani, a déclaré dimanche son directeur général, Giuseppe Marsocci. Airbus recule après un défaut de qualité sur des A321neo L'action Airbus reculait vendredi, l'avionneur européen ayant annoncé la veille avoir identifié un défaut de qualité susceptible d'affecter des centaines de ses appareils à succès de type A321neo. Le financement de l'IA fait peser des risques systémiques sur l'économie américaine selon une étude Le développement de l’intelligence artificielle devrait, à terme, mobiliser une part plus importante de la production américaine que ne l'avait fait le déploiement du réseau électrique, des chemins de fer, des autoroutes inter-États ou encore d’internet, avec une structure financière de plus en plus complexe présentant des risques potentiellement systémiques, selon une étude universitaire à paraître vendredi. Zone euro: La croissance des prêts aux entreprises ralentit en août, selon la BCE La croissance des prêts aux entreprises dans la zone euro a ralenti en août, montrent les données publiées vendredi par la Banque centrale européenne (BCE). Allemagne: Le moral des consommateurs devrait se dégrader plus que prévu, selon GfK Le moral des consommateurs allemands devrait se dégrader plus que prévu à l'approche du mois d'octobre, montre une enquête publiée vendredi. ArcelorMittal prévoit une charge de $1 md après des frappes sur son aciérie de Kryvyi Rih en Ukraine ArcelorMittal a annoncé vendredi ne pas être en mesure de relancer l'activité de son aciérie ukrainienne de Kryvyi Rih, touchée par des frappes de missiles le 21 septembre, le groupe anticipant une charge de dépréciation hors flux de trésorerie d'environ un milliard de dollars (878,35 millions d'euros).

item.title: OFRTP Summary
item.description: A Metz, séquence européenne pour le pape Léon XIV et Emmanuel Macron
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A Metz, séquence européenne pour le pape Léon XIV et Emmanuel Macron METZ, Moselle, 28 septembre (Reuters) - Le pape Léon XIV conclut ce lundi sa tournée en France par une dernière étape à Metz, non loin de la frontière allemande, pour une séquence dédiée à l'Europe et à la paix en présence du président Emmanuel Macron. Bombardements russes meurtriers sur Kyiv et Dnipro KYIV, 28 septembre (Reuters) - L'armée russe a de nouveau bombardé Kyiv lundi, visant plusieurs cibles dont le bâtiment de l'Académie des Sciences, dans le centre de la capitale, où le maire Vitali Klitchko déplore un mort et 19 blessés. Royaume-Uni: Cinq suspects d'un projet d'attentat contre une base de la RAF libérés sous caution FAIRFORD, Angleterre, 28 septembre (Reuters) - La police britannique a interrogé lundi cinq hommes suspectés de projet terroriste avant d'annoncer leur libération sous caution, au lendemain de leur interpellation près d'une base aérienne utilisée par les États-Unis pour mener des frappes contre l'Iran. Andersson dit ne pas pouvoir former un gouvernement, Kristersson revient dans le jeu STOCKHOLM, 28 septembre (Reuters) - La présidente du Parti social-démocrate suédois, Magdalena Andersson, a annoncé lundi ne pas être en mesure d'obtenir un soutien suffisant pour former un nouveau gouvernement après la courte victoire du bloc de centre-gauche aux élections législatives du 13 septembre. Le Rassemblement national aura un groupe au Sénat, une première PARIS, 27 septembre (Reuters) - Le Rassemblement national sera en mesure de composer un groupe au Sénat, soit au moins 10 élus, ce qui sera une première pour la formation d'extrême-droite, à l'issue des élections sénatoriales de ce dimanche qui a vu le renouvellement de la moitié des sièges de la Chambre haute du Parlement. Le pape Léon XIV a passé deux heures avec des victimes de violences sexuelles commises par des prêtres Le pape Léon XIV a rencontré des victimes de violences sexuelles commises par des prêtres dimanche, lors de sa visite à Lourdes, après avoir exhorté l'Église catholique à reconnaître ses défaillances et à panser les "blessures profondes" infligées en son sein. La moitié des sièges du Sénat renouvelée, le RN espère un groupe La moitié du Sénat français est renouvelée ce dimanche lors d'élections au suffrage universel indirect dont l'un des principaux enjeux est la capacité du Rassemblement national (RN) à constituer un groupe, soit au moins dix élus. Le pape Léon XIV parle "d'espérance" lors d'une messe géante au coeur de Paris Une messe géante au coeur de Paris a constitué samedi le moment fort du deuxième jour de la tournée en France du pape Léon XIV, accueilli sur l'avenue des Champs-Elysées par une foule nombreuse, joyeuse et recueillie. L'aéroport de Catane de nouveau fermé à cause des cendres de l'Etna Les vols à l'aéroport de Catane, en Sicile, ont de nouveau été suspendus samedi en raison des cendres générées par l'Etna, le volcan le plus haut et le plus actif d'Europe, qui avait déjà perturbé l'activité de l'aéroport plus tôt dans le mois et en août, a annoncé l'opérateur de l'infrastructure. A Paris, Léon XIV délivre des messages sur la paix, la fin de vie et le "paradis des machines" Le pape Léon XIV a délivré vendredi des messages de paix et de dignité humaine, s'inquiétant de "perdre notre humanité au milieu du paradis des machines" au premier jour de sa visite de quatre jours en France, "terre de riches racines chrétiennes".
